title: Spacing Effects in Learning: A Temporal Ridgeline of Optimal Retention https://laplab.ucsd.edu/articles/Cepeda%20et%20al%202008_psychsci.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 1, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Cepeda and colleagues' large study, over 1,300 participants, that pins down how the ideal gap between study sessions relates to how long material needs to be remembered. Their key finding is a temporal ridgeline — for any given retention interval there's an optimal gap, and that optimal gap grows the longer you need to remember something, with roughly a 21-day optimal gap for one-year retention. Barton draws out the clear practical framing: teachers should ask how long they need students to remember something before deciding how to schedule review, and the paper's evidence suggests the costs of spacing too far apart are much smaller than the costs of spacing too close together, i.e. cramming. This directly challenges the intuitive appeal of concentrated revision blocks before exams.
points: There's an optimal gap between study sessions for any target retention length, and that gap grows the longer you want students to remember the material — for a year-long retention target, the optimal gap was around 21 days.
Cramming produces high immediate mastery that doesn't last — a single intense week of study is unlikely to translate into long-term retention.
The downside of spacing sessions too far apart is much smaller than the downside of spacing them too close together, so when in doubt, err toward longer gaps.
Teachers should explicitly plan review schedules around the question of how long the material needs to be remembered, rather than defaulting to a fixed revision timetable.
quotes: The findings indicate that an optimal gap exists for each retention interval, and this optimal gap increases with the length of the retention interval.

The results suggest that conventional educational practices that cram learning into short periods might be inefficient and lead to poor long-term retention, while spacing study sessions strategically can significantly improve memory performance.
The optimal gap between study sessions is not an absolute value, but depends on how long students need to remember the information.
Cramming information into a short period is likely to lead to high levels of immediate mastery, but this mastery will not last.
While there are disadvantages to having a gap that is longer than the optimal value, these are much smaller than the disadvantages of having a gap that is too short.
To put it simply, if you want to know the optimal distribution of study time, you need to decide how long you wish to remember something
